words.d: player versus player, or players versus the game's enemies
cooperative play: players working together toward a shared goal
playing at the same time in real time, or taking turns at different times
the system that picks who plays against whom
ruining other players' fun on purpose
a group of players who team up long-term
a hidden skill rating used to match players of similar skill

cards.text: When humans play together, even co-op games turn competitive. Before designing multiplayer, decide **how players connect** and **how they relate**: compete, cooperate, or share a space with different goals.
In the arcade game Gauntlet, four players were supposed to cooperate. Rogers and his friends shoved each other to grab the health food first. Scarce rewards create rivalry.
Put a shared chest with a "first to claim" rule into a co-op event, and a friendly team turns into rivals. Decide on purpose which feeling you want.
Mobile multiplayer runs through a server that decides what's true, so a hacked phone can't give itself gems. Playing on the same couch became party invites, friend codes and clanmates.
Co-op is just competition that hasn't found the health potion yet.

check.q: What turned Gauntlet's co-op into competition?
check.why: When rewards are limited, teammates start competing for them.

cards.text: Multiplayer modes are a menu of motivations. **Each mode answers: what do players want from each other?** Combine and rotate them for variety.

Some classic modes:
- deathmatch: everyone for themselves
- team battles and capture the flag
- survival against waves of enemies
- territory control
- co-op missions, racing and virtual life
Brawl Stars keeps the same heroes fresh by rotating which modes and maps are live. The "variety of modes" rule became an event calendar.
Let players create content if you can: user-made maps and modes give free content, longer life and new ways to play. Roblox is built entirely on this.

check.q: How does Brawl Stars keep its heroes feeling fresh?
check.why: Rotating modes changes how the same heroes play.

lessons.title: Don't let the rich get richer

cards.text: **Systems that reward the leader** make the leader snowball, and everyone else gives up. **Systems that help those behind** keep races tense.
Racing games often give better items to players at the back, so the race stays close. Rewarding the leader with even more power ends the contest early.
In F2P, money can become the snowball. If big spenders crush free players, the free players leave. Then the spenders have no one to play against.
Use matchmaking brackets, caps and fair matching to protect free players. Games with dice, slots or gacha also need ethics: show the odds, add pity systems, and never target minors.

check.q: Why is pay-to-win dangerous even for spenders?
options: Free players leave, and spenders lose their opponents
check.why: Free players are the content. If they quit, the game empties for everyone.

cards.text: There's no magic number. **The right player count is whatever your core gameplay needs.** Too many breaks a duel. Too few makes a world feel empty.
A fighting game like Street Fighter gets messy with more than two players: characters bunch up and nobody can see what's happening. World of Warcraft would feel empty with only a few hundred players.

Hidden mobile limit: **matchmaking liquidity**. Every extra player per match means more people must be online at the same skill level. A 100-player mode in a small game means long waits and players quitting.
Ask three questions: How many people does the fun need? How many can my audience supply at 3 a.m. in a small country? How many can a thumb track on a phone screen?
Two players in a huge world is a ghost town. Two hundred in a duel is a mosh pit.

options: Having enough players online to fill matches quickly
check.why: Bigger matches need more waiting players, which small games may not have.

lessons.title: The social toolkit from online RPGs

cards.text: Big online RPGs (MMORPGs) invented a **social toolkit** that players now expect, and F2P inherited it: guilds, raids, crafting, trading, collections and player housing.
These systems fill out a game and keep people together for years. Without them, an online game feels thin.
Zynga's Facebook games like Mafia Wars pioneered asking friends for gifts to unlock content. Candy Crush asking friends for lives is a direct descendant.

Players used to sell game gold for real money, which developers hated. F2P turned that into the business model: the publisher sells the currency. Avoid upgrades that can fail and destroy expensive items. Never punish twice.

check.q: Where did Candy Crush's "ask friends for lives" idea come from?
options: Early Facebook social games like Mafia Wars
check.why: Friend gifting gates were pioneered by Facebook social games.

cards.text: Other people can make a game heaven or hell. **Design fences against the dark side of human nature**: griefing, spawn camping and rich-get-richer systems.

- **Griefing:** ruining others' fun on purpose.
- **Spawn camping:** waiting where players reappear and attacking them instantly.
Fixes: short protection after respawn, reporting tools, and limits on harmful actions.
Clash of Clans gives you a shield after you're attacked, so you can't be raided again and again while you're offline.
Give clan leaders moderation tools: kick, promote, minimum requirements and written rules. Good communities need good tools.
Make other people heaven most of the time, and build fences for the rest.

check.q: Why does Clash of Clans give a shield after an attack?
options: So players aren't attacked over and over
check.why: It protects players from griefing while they can't defend themselves.

lessons.title: Players will do the last thing you expect

cards.text: Give players tools and other humans, and **they will invent behaviour you never designed.** Embrace the creative stuff. Shut down anything that ruins other people's fun.

Good surprises: self-made challenges, friendly clan tournaments, shared base layouts. Bad surprises (exploits): win-trading, multiple accounts feeding one main account, bots, and cheating rewards by changing the phone clock.
Before any multiplayer event launches, ask: "How would a bored 14-year-old with three accounts abuse this?"
Tools: the server checks every important action, limits on gifting, alerts for strange economy numbers, and a switch to turn off a broken event instantly.
Players are raccoons. They'll open every bin you thought was sealed.

check.q: Which is an exploit to stop quickly?
options: Using extra accounts to feed a main account
check.why: Exploits ruin fairness for others. Creative play is fine.

cards.text: In mobile F2P, **other players are your cheapest, most renewable content.** Choose between **sync** (playing at the same time) and **async** (playing at different times).
Async is the default for casual and mid-core players: you attack someone's base while they're offline. Sync is for games where the fun is real-time skill, like Brawl Stars. Many games mix both.
Mobile connections lag, so real-time duels moved to designs that tolerate delay: Clash Royale's elixir pace, or fighting against an AI-controlled copy of another player's team.
If your audience plays in short bursts on the bus, async multiplayer fits better. Nobody wants to wait three minutes in a queue.

check.q: Raiding someone's base while they're offline is which type?
check.why: The players don't have to be online at the same time.

cards.text: Social bonds are the **strongest predictor of long-term retention.** A player who quits a solo game quits a game. A player who quits a clan quits friends.

Clan features:
- **help requests:** donate troops or cards, speed up a friend's timer
- **clan wars:** clan against clan
- **co-op bosses:** fight a big boss together
- **team events:** everyone's wins fill a shared chest
Clash of Clans has Clan Wars and Clan Games. Clash Royale has card donations. Monopoly GO! has partner events, where you build toward a shared goal with friends.
Unlock clans after the player understands the basics, then push them gently to join one. A player in an active clan is far less likely to quit.

check.q: Why do clans improve retention so much?
options: Players feel responsible to teammates and friends
check.why: Obligation and friendship keep people coming back.

cards.text: Competitive games need a **visible ladder** to climb and a **hidden rating** that makes matches fair.

- **Trophies or ranks** show progress to the player.
- A hidden **MMR** matches players of similar skill.
- **Seasons** reset ranks a little, so everyone gets a fresh climb and a seasonal reward.
Clash Royale's trophy road climbs through arenas, and each new arena unlocks new cards. The ladder is also a progression system.
Many games fill low-rank matches with bots, so new players aren't crushed and queues stay short. Be careful: players notice obvious bots, and too many feel fake.

check.q: Why do competitive games use seasons?
options: To give everyone a fresh climb and a reward
check.why: Seasonal resets renew motivation to climb again.
